query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A single intervention of applying cryogenic rolling followed by a tailored low‐temperature annealing treatment to as‐cast eutectic HEAs (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) will simultaneously increase strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast eutectic high-entropy alloys with lamellar microstructures composed of a soft FCC phase and a hard BCC phase/intermetallic compound.
generation.intervention: Cryogenic rolling (performed at liquid nitrogen temperatures) immediately followed by a controlled annealing treatment at a temperature low enough to recover ductility without significant microstructural coarsening.
generation.conditions: The treatment is applied under controlled deformation conditions at cryogenic temperatures, with annealing performed at a moderate temperature (around 600°C) for a short duration, and subsequent tensile tests conducted at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction in lamellar spacing, increased and refined dislocation density, and improved phase interfaces between the soft and hard phases.
generation.mechanism: Cryogenic rolling refines the microstructure and increases dislocation density without excessive dynamic recovery while ensuring higher stored energy, and the subsequent annealing allows for controlled recrystallization/recovery primarily at interphase boundaries. This combination enhances work-hardening capacity and delays necking, thus simultaneously increasing strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated as-cast baseline, the intervention is expected to yield samples with an approximate 20–30% increase in yield strength and a maintenance or modest increase in ductility (e.g., elongation improvements), though exact gains will vary with composition and processing parameters.
generation.baseline: As-cast eutectic HEAs processed without any specialized thermo-mechanical treatment (i.e., without cryogenic rolling and tailored annealing).
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only if the processing parameters are optimized to avoid unwanted phase instability or coarsening. Compositions significantly different from the studied eutectic systems or with extremely high/low contents of key elements (e.g., Cr) might not show the same outcome.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantification of strength and ductility gains is uncertain and may depend on the exact alloy composition and process parameters. Further optimization may be necessary to consistently achieve the simultaneous property improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples with identical composition. Subject one set to cryogenic rolling followed by the tailored annealing treatment, and maintain the other set as a control (either as-cast or conventionally processed without cryogenic rolling). Characterize both sets using tensile tests, electron microscopy (TEM/EBSD) for microstructural analysis, and dislocation density measurements.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both strength (e.g., yield/ultimate strength) and ductility (e.g., total elongation) compared to the control samples under identical testing conditions.

cited_evidence.text: The higher content of Cr helps the resistance of the local deformation response, improving the nonuniform strain and promoting the balance of strength and ductility of the alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, microstructure, mechanical property, work-hardening behavior

To tackle the aforementioned problems, eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [] were proposed. On the one hand, EHEAs should have the general character of traditional eutectic alloys. In this sense, EHEAs should have better fluidity and thus better castability and less casting defects [,]. On the other hand, EHEAs as one kind of in-situ composites with lamellar or rod-like eutectic microstructures might reach the balance between strength and ductility via mixing the soft FCC phase with the hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound [,,,,,,,,]. Some EHEAs indeed have outstanding properties. Lu et al. [] reported the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with simultaneous high strength (944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6%). The excellent mechanical properties do not depend significantly on derivation of eutectic compositions []. After cold-rolling and annealing, its strength reached up to 1.2 GPa and its elongation could remain at about 12% []. After cryo-rolling and annealing, its strength could reach up to 1.47 GPa while its ductility could even increase to 14% []. He et al. [,] designed the CoCrFeNiNbx EHEAs and found that the microstructures were stable from 600 °C to 900 °C.
